findings.headline: All new borrowing is short-term from other local authorities; no long-term PWLB funding accessed
findings.detail: Council has taken £58m net new borrowing entirely via 6-12 month loans from other councils at 4.2%-4.8%. No new long-term fixed-rate PWLB borrowing has been undertaken, creating potential refinancing risk if short-term markets tighten.
findings.matters: Reliance on short-term inter-authority borrowing exposes the council to rollover risk and interest rate exposure; prevents locking in long-term fixed rates.
findings.figures: £58m net new short-term borrowing from other councils at 4.2%-4.8% rates; £0 new long-term PWLB borrowing
findings.quote: The Council has not undertaken any new long-term fixed-rate maturity loans from PWLB during the first quarter of the year. Some short-term borrowing from other Local Authorities has taken place as the interest rate has proved advantageous at this time

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account capital works delayed following Morgan Sindall contract extension
findings.detail: The largest component of the £9.1m capital underspend in Q1 is HRA, where planned works have not started on schedule. HRA capital expenditure stands at £(47)k actual against a £10.8m budget, representing a £10.8m favorable variance driven entirely by the delay.
findings.matters: Capital delivery delays indicate execution risk and could signal further slippage; affects council's ability to meet tenant needs and asset management targets.
findings.figures: HRA capital actuals £(47)k vs working budget £10,792k; variance £(10,839)k
findings.quote: The most significant variance relates to the Housing Revenue Account (HRA), where the commencement of planned works has been delayed following the extension of the Morgan Sindall contract.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 Internal Audit & Counter Fraud Progress Update 2026/27 (1)
findings.headline: Housing Disrepair audit identified major control gaps on Pre-Action Protocol and Awaab's Law compliance, due September 2026
findings.detail: A Major priority recommendation requires the Housing Disrepair Policy to be updated to reflect current practice and reference the Pre-Action Protocol for Housing Conditions Claims and Awaab's Law (mandatory building safety standard). The recommendation is still pending and now due 30 September 2026. The council is also seeking to establish 'a sustainable and adequately resourced operating model' to manage disrepair cases, suggesting current capacity or process failure.
findings.matters: Awaab's Law compliance is a statutory duty for housing maintenance; gaps here expose the council to regulatory enforcement, tenant litigation, and liability. Poor resource allocation to disrepair cases signals inability to manage a core housing function.
findings.figures: Due date: 30-Sep-2026; Awaab's Law reference required
findings.quote: The Housing Disrepair Policy, and associated workflows will be updated to reflect current practice and reference the Pre-Action Protocol for Housing Conditions Claims, and Awaab's Law.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 Internal Audit & Counter Fraud Progress Update 2026/27 (1)
findings.headline: Multiple Major priority audit recommendations on housing leaseholder charging have slipped, with Property Services restructure now pending
findings.detail: Seven Major priority recommendations on Section 20 Leaseholder Charges (from 2025/26 audit) remain outstanding as of August 2026. Issues include leaseholders being recharged for works not yet completed, inconsistent timing of invoices, and lack of IT systems support. All are dependent on a Property Asset Strategy Service restructure 'due to be completed within the next six to eight months'. These represent material customer-facing service failures and financial exposure.
findings.matters: Leaseholder charging disputes and delays suggest customer trust issues and create legal/reputational risk; systemic failures waiting for a restructure indicate the council is unable to fix known problems quickly and may indicate wider service delivery weakness.
findings.figures: 7 Major recommendations; restructure timeline: 6-8 months from May 2026
findings.quote: The recharging process for major/planned works will be reviewed as leaseholders should only be recharged when the works are completed and the accounts finalised to ensure all costs are known and included. Costs should not be carried over from year to year.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 Internal Audit & Counter Fraud Progress Update 2026/27 (1)
findings.headline: Housing Repairs transition includes limited-scope investigation into payments, suggesting controls or fraud concerns
findings.detail: An audit of Housing Repairs Transition is listed as a Priority 1 audit with a 'Limited-scope investigation into payments made' under Deborah Fenton and David White. This is not a routine audit but specifically targets payment integrity in a transition context, flagging potential control or fraud risk.
findings.matters: An investigation into housing repair payments during service transition suggests prior control failures or fraud concerns that could indicate cash leakage or vendor management risk in a material service.
findings.figures: Housing Repairs audit scope: payments investigation
findings.quote: Housing Repairs Limited-scope investigation into payments made.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 Internal Audit & Counter Fraud Progress Update 2026/27 (1)
findings.headline: Audit recommendations overdue backlog jumped from 14 to 28 in one month, suggesting governance control breakdown
findings.detail: In July 2026, 14 audit recommendations were overdue (39% of 71 active); by August 10th, this had doubled to 28 overdue (39% still, but on a growing base). Three are Major priority and 24 are Moderate. The document notes managers are not consistently providing updates or evidence, requiring Internal Audit to chase them. Repeated delays undermine the control environment.
findings.matters: A lender relies on audit oversight to catch control failures early; a doubling of overdue recommendations in one month and managers avoiding accountability suggests weakening governance that could hide larger financial or operational problems.
findings.figures: 14 overdue in July; 28 overdue as of 10/08/2026; 71 total active recommendations; 3 Major, 24 Moderate overdue
findings.quote: As of 10/08/2026, there were 71 active audit recommendations recorded in Pentana. Of these, 51 (72%) are overdue based on their original implementation dates (date agreed in final report). However, when considering the revised implementation dates, the number of overdue recommendations drops to 28 (39%); 3 classified as 'Major', 24 classified as 'Moderate' priority and 1 'Low' priority. At the time of last reporting, back in July, this figure was 14

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 Internal Audit & Counter Fraud Progress Update 2026/27 (1)
findings.headline: Housing funding lost due to council receiving C4 performance rating on housing stock condition
findings.detail: Basildon was assessed as C4 on its Housing function in relation to existing stock, resulting in withdrawal of envisaged funding for the Housing Programme. This audit review was therefore removed from the plan. The C4 rating directly triggered loss of capital funding the council had planned to use.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can deliver on its housing obligations and maintain asset quality; a C4 rating and funding loss suggests performance shortfalls that could affect revenue-generating housing activities and tenant-related income.
findings.figures: C4 rating; Housing Programme funding withdrawn
findings.quote: Envisaged funding is no longer available to Basildon Council due to the poor rating (C4) awarded to its Housing function in relation to its existing stock.

findings.headline: Government announced review of the Council's governance arrangements
findings.detail: The committee noted that government announced a review of the council's governance arrangements on the day of this meeting (15 July 2026). The AGS and work programme were updated to reflect this external review, which has potential implications for the council's governance arrangements.
findings.matters: Government-initiated review of governance arrangements signals external concern about the council's governance and indicates potential intervention or remedial requirements.
findings.figures: none
findings.quote: Government's announcement earlier that day concerning a review of the Council's governance arrangements

findings.headline: Recurring audit findings over two years have not been remedied despite management action plans
findings.detail: Members expressed concern that control weaknesses identified by Internal Audit have been repeatedly reported over several years with limited evidence of sustained improvement. Internal Audit had consistently highlighted governance and control concerns for at least two years, yet committee noted the recurring nature of issues and emphasised the importance of ensuring recommendations are implemented in a timely manner.
findings.matters: Persistent unresolved audit findings over multiple years suggest weak management capability and governance accountability, increasing organisational and financial risk.
findings.figures: at least two years
findings.quote: Internal Audit had consistently highlighted these concerns for at least two years through reports to both management and the Committee

findings.headline: Capital expenditure significantly underspent at £71.3m against £139.1m budget
findings.detail: Capital expenditure for 2025/26 was £71.3m against a working budget of £139.1m (49% underspend). The majority of unspent budget is being carried forward to support ongoing projects. This could indicate delivery capacity constraints or project delays.
findings.matters: Large capital underspends can signal project delivery challenges or capacity constraints relevant to the council's ability to execute its capital programme.
findings.figures: £71.3m against working budget of £139.1m
findings.quote: capital expenditure for the year totalled £71.3m against a working budget of £139.1m, with the majority of unspent budget to be carried forward to support ongoing projects

findings.headline: Annual Governance Statement identifies financial sustainability as a significant governance issue
findings.detail: The 2025/26 AGS explicitly identified financial sustainability as one of several significant governance issues, alongside housing services, member conduct arrangements, organisational capacity and compliance with governance processes. The statement notes that governance frameworks are not operating consistently enough to be fully effective.
findings.matters: An explicit statement in the council's own governance assessment that financial sustainability is a significant concern is a material red flag for lenders.
findings.figures: none
findings.quote: The AGS identified a number of significant governance issues, including housing services, financial sustainability, member conduct arrangements, organisational capacity and compliance with governance processes.

findings.headline: Limited Assurance audit opinion issued for second consecutive year
findings.detail: The council received an overall opinion of Limited Assurance for 2025/26, the second year running. The opinion reflects systemic issues rather than isolated concerns, with recurring findings across governance compliance, risk management, project management, housing services and implementation of audit recommendations. Internal Audit has consistently highlighted these concerns for at least two years.
findings.matters: Consecutive years of limited assurance indicate systemic control and governance weaknesses that affect the council's financial management capability and risk profile.
findings.figures: second consecutive year
findings.quote: for the second consecutive year, an overall opinion of Limited Assurance had been issued

findings.headline: Heavy reliance on temporary borrowing (35% of total) with material forward deals pending
findings.detail: Of £518m total borrowing, £183m is temporary borrowing from other councils. A further £55m in forward deals are already arranged. This creates ongoing refinancing dependency and exposure to rate movements on short-term facilities.
findings.matters: Councils dependent on temporary borrowing face liquidity pressure if refinancing becomes harder or rates spike; this is material given 63% of new borrowing in the quarter was temporary
findings.figures: Temporary borrowing £183m (35% of total); forward LA borrowing deals £55m; 10 new temporary loans of £58m in Q1

findings.headline: Temporary borrowing interest costs are running 63% over budget for the quarter
findings.detail: In Q1, the council spent £1,924,636 on temporary loan interest against a quarterly budget of approximately £1,180,650. Annualizing this run-rate gives £7.7m against a full-year budget of £4.7m. This suggests interest costs on short-term borrowing are materially higher than planned.
findings.matters: Unexplained cost overruns on interest reduce financial headroom and signal either higher-than-expected borrowing rates or larger borrowing volumes than budgeted
findings.figures: Q1 actual £1,924,636 vs full-year budget £4,722,600; annualized run-rate £7.7m
findings.quote: Short Term Borrowing: Temporary Loan 4,722,600 1,924,636 (2,797,964)

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn 2025/26 and Budget Setting Process 2027/28
findings.headline: Basildon's 2027/28 budget setting explicitly targets closing a structural "budget gap identified in future years," with savings still to be identified and inflation applied cautiously
findings.detail: The report outlines that "the budget approach will as always focus on trying to address the budget gap identified in future years." The council plans to identify savings, apply inflation only to contractually obligated expenditure (not to all budgets), maintain a 2.5% pay award provision, and increase fees and charges by minimum CPI. This language indicates a structural funding gap is expected to persist.
findings.matters: A structural budget gap—where recurring expenditure structurally exceeds recurring income—must be closed by recurring savings or income growth. If savings targets are not met (as the 2025/26 pattern suggests), reserves will continue to decline. A lender assesses whether the council has a credible plan to close the gap sustainably.
findings.figures: Gap is described as "identified" but no specific amount given in this document
findings.quote: the budget approach will as always focus on trying to address the budget gap identified in future years.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn 2025/26 and Budget Setting Process 2027/28
findings.headline: Despite the £5m mid-year budget amendment, Basildon's actual outturn deteriorated by £0.7m compared to the Period 8 forecast, with Capital Financing overspend identified as the most notable factor
findings.detail: At Period 8 (month 8), the council forecast a £5.7m overspend. It added £5.0m to the budget to address this, expecting the outturn to improve to roughly breakeven. However, the actual outturn was £1.4m overspent. The paper explains: "This variation is due to a range of factors, most notably an overspend on Capital Financing. This has been partially offset by a combination of small improvements across multiple services as well as a significant improvement in previously estimated income levels in Planning."
findings.matters: This pattern—mid-year forecast inaccuracy followed by further deterioration despite corrective action—suggests the council's forecasting capability is challenged. If Period 8 estimates were off, later forecasts for 2026/27 and the 2027/28 budget-setting may also be unreliable, particularly concerning given the paper notes homelessness and capital financing costs "will remain as potential future risks."
findings.figures: Period 8 forecast overspend £5.7m; budget amendment £5.0m; actual outturn £1.4m; deterioration vs Period 8 forecast £0.7m
findings.quote: The £1.4m overspend suggests an improvement of £4.3m compared to the £5.7m overspend reported at Period 8 . However, when taking into account the £5.0m approved through the 2026/27 budget report to address the previously reported forecast overspend and reflected in the working budget position, then the outturn position has in fact deteriorated by £0.7m since that Period 8.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn 2025/26 and Budget Setting Process 2027/28
findings.headline: Basildon's un-ringfenced reserves fell by £7.2m net over 2025/26, with the General Fund available balance now at £3.0m and HRA available reserves at £1.971m
findings.detail: Total reserves decreased from £44.965m (opening) to £36.769m (General Fund available after carry forwards), with HRA reserves falling from £9.889m to £6.271m available. The paper records: "considering th e £5.0m already taken from reserves earlier in the year, there was a n overall net decrease in un -ringfenced reserves for 2025/26." Despite embedding higher temporary accommodation and capital financing budgets into 2026/27 and forward years, the council still ran a deficit.
findings.matters: Reserves are a council's buffer against volatility and unforeseen costs. A lender assesses reserve adequacy relative to budget size and risk profile. Drawing £5m mid-year to patch an identified risk, then overspending that by a further £1.4m, suggests reserves are being drawn to manage structural issues rather than temporary volatility.
findings.figures: Opening reserves £44.965m; closing available £36.769m General Fund and £6.271m HRA; net decrease £7.215m
findings.quote: However, considering th e £5.0m already taken from reserves earlier in the year, there was a n overall net decrease in un -ringfenced reserves for 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn 2025/26 and Budget Setting Process 2027/28
findings.headline: Basildon's HRA swung from a budgeted surplus of £1.6m to a £3.6m deficit, driven by responsive repairs, legal disrepair claims, and damp-and-mould cases
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account saw expenditure £2.5m over budget and income £0.8m below budget. The overspend was "largely driven by responsive repairs, legal disrepair claims and damp and mould cases." Rental income fell because of "longer void periods resulting from extensive repair works required before properties could be re-let"—indicating substantial repair backlogs are preventing properties from generating income. This deficit is covered from HRA reserves due to ring-fencing.
findings.matters: Legal disrepair cases represent crystallised contingent liabilities. A backlog of responsive repairs affecting void periods signals deteriorating asset condition and deferred maintenance costs now coming due. For a lender, this indicates future capital spending will be elevated and rental income generation is impaired.
findings.figures: HRA deficit £3.6m vs budgeted surplus of £1.6m (£5.2m swing); repairs overspend £4.581m
findings.quote: The adverse outturn is largely driven by responsive repairs, legal disrepair claims and damp and mould cases. Rental income and Service charges were lower than budgeted due to longer void periods resulting from extensive repair works required before properties could be re-let.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn 2025/26 and Budget Setting Process 2027/28
findings.headline: Basildon added £5m mid-year to address temporary accommodation pressures driven by homelessness duties, then overspent by a further £1.4m despite this
findings.detail: The council's initial period 8 forecast showed a £5.7m overspend. In response, Basildon added £5.0m to its working budget specifically to address "increasing cost of temporary accommodation to cover our statutory duty around homelessness." Despite this top-up, the actual outturn was still £1.4m overspent, meaning the position deteriorated by £0.7m from the Period 8 forecast. The paper acknowledges this will "remain as potential future risks to the budget if demand for temporary accommodation grows further than anticipated."
findings.matters: Homelessness-driven temporary accommodation costs are legally mandated but volatile in volume and price. A lender needs to understand whether costs are stabilising or continuing to escalate. The pattern here—mid-year emergency amendment plus continued deterioration—suggests the council lacks predictive control over this cost.
findings.figures: £5.0m added to budget mid-year; £1.4m outturn overspend; £0.7m deterioration from Period 8 forecast
findings.quote: There were significant pressures arising in 2025/26 namely within Housing, driven by increasing cost of temporary accommodation to cover our statutory duty around homelessness, alongside pressures in Capital Financing.

findings.paper_title: CAPITAL AND INVESTMENT STRATEGY ANNUAL REPORT AND PRUDENTIAL INDICATORS 2025/26
findings.paper_url: https://www.basildonmeetings.info/documents/s158414/Capital and Investment Strategy Annual Report And Prudential Indicators 202526 15072026 Audit an.pdf
findings.headline: Financing cost ratios are increasing and pressuring medium-term financial sustainability
findings.detail: Both absolute financing costs and the ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream have increased in 2025/26. The council identifies this as a risk that may place further pressure on medium-term financial sustainability, requiring continued monitoring.
findings.matters: Rising debt service costs as a proportion of revenue is a key affordability metric; trends upward suggest the council's capacity to service debt is shrinking relative to operational budget.
findings.figures: Specific ratios and amounts not detailed in this cover report; metrics in Enclosure No. 2 (Treasury Management Performance Dashboard) and Enclosure No. 3 (Prudential Indicators)
findings.quote: increases in financing costs and the ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream may place further pressure on the Council's medium-term financial sustainability

findings.paper_title: CAPITAL AND INVESTMENT STRATEGY ANNUAL REPORT AND PRUDENTIAL INDICATORS 2025/26
findings.paper_url: https://www.basildonmeetings.info/documents/s158414/Capital and Investment Strategy Annual Report And Prudential Indicators 202526 15072026 Audit an.pdf
findings.headline: Capital programme slippage is delaying project delivery and increasing costs
findings.detail: The council's capital programme experienced slippage in 2025/26 that delays achievement of corporate objectives, increases project costs, and affects timely delivery of anticipated benefits. This is identified as the most significant risk from the year's outturn.
findings.matters: Delayed capital projects affect service delivery timing and cost control; overruns strain the council's financial sustainability and may indicate project management or funding issues.
findings.figures: Specific amounts not quantified in this cover report; detail in Enclosure No. 1 (Capital and Investment Strategy Annual Report)
findings.quote: The most significant relate to the delivery of the capital programme, where slippage may delay the achievement of corporate objectives, increase project costs and affect the timely delivery of anticipated benefits.

findings.headline: Housing regulatory compliance and tenant safety is a governance failure
findings.detail: The council lists 'Housing regulatory compliance and tenant safety' as a primary area where governance has weakened. No detail of the specific breach is given in this summary, but the council acknowledges failure to maintain compliance.
findings.matters: Housing compliance failures create regulatory fines, reputational damage, and potential financial liability—direct risks to council finances.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Housing regulatory compliance and tenant safety

findings.headline: Leadership stability is uncertain; council cannot yet conclude governance framework is fully effective
findings.detail: The council states: 'the Council cannot yet conclude that its governance framework is fully embedded and operating effectively in all respects'. It identifies 'Organisational capacity and leadership stability' as a weakness, and recovery depends on 'continued leadership stability'—language suggesting stability is currently at risk.
findings.matters: Leadership instability or turnover affects a council's ability to execute financial plans and maintain control discipline—a direct concern for lenders assessing execution risk.
findings.figures: 8 governance areas identified as requiring improvement; 38 governance areas total assessed
findings.quote: the Council cannot yet conclude that its governance framework is fully embedded and operating effectively in all respects

findings.headline: Financial sustainability and medium-term resilience identified as a governance weakness
findings.detail: The council names 'Financial sustainability and medium-term resilience' as one of eight significant areas where its governance arrangements are not yet consistently effective and require improvement. No specific financial detail is provided, but this is the council's own assessment that its governance over financial sustainability needs strengthening.
findings.matters: A lender assessing risk needs to know a council recognises its own governance weaknesses in financial sustainability; this statement indicates Basildon does, and is taking action to improve.
findings.figures: None provided for the financial sustainability issue specifically
findings.quote: Financial sustainability and medium-term resilience

findings.headline: Housing service transition to in-house model rated red; regulator gave C4 grading (serious failings) immediately prior
findings.detail: The transition from long-term outsourced housing repairs to the new Basildon Better Homes in-house model is rated red due to 'significant governance, delivery and reputational risks.' The move introduces 'high level of operational complexity, with the potential for service disruption, increased costs and reduced resident satisfaction.' This is compounded by the Housing Regulator's C4 grading, which indicates 'serious failings requiring fundamental improvement.'
findings.matters: A service transition carrying high operational risk, combined with a regulator finding of serious failings, creates both immediate disruption risk and medium-term reputational/financial risk. Service failures or cost overruns during transition would directly impact the council's revenue budget and regulatory standing.
findings.figures: Housing Regulator grading: C4 (serious failings requiring fundamental improvement)
findings.quote: Service Disruption and Reputational Damage During Housing Repairs Transition is rated red due to the significant governance, delivery and reputational risks associated with the transition to the Basildon Better Homes service model... This is further heightened by the outcome of the Housing Regulator inspection, where the Council received a C4 grading, indicating serious failings requiring fundamental improvement.

findings.headline: Homelessness and temporary accommodation costs creating significant and growing revenue pressure
findings.detail: The council rates the sustainability of housing and homelessness services as amber due to rising delivery costs and funding uncertainty. It explicitly identifies temporary accommodation funding as a 'significant and growing pressure' on the revenue budget that contributes directly to financial sustainability risks. Demand remains volatile and difficult to forecast.
findings.matters: Homelessness and temporary accommodation are demand-led pressures that erode financial resilience. A growing cost driver that contributes to the council's inability to close its budget gap indicates a structural revenue problem that does not resolve on its own.
findings.figures: No specific cost figures provided in this report
findings.quote: The financial implications of homelessness, particularly the provision of temporary accommodation, present a significant and growing pressure on the Council's revenue budget. This contributes directly to wider financial sustainability risks, as rising costs and volatile demand make it more difficult to deliver planned savings and maintain a stable financial position.

findings.headline: Material savings delivery failures already identified and MTFS cannot yet close the budget gap
findings.detail: The council's medium-term financial strategy does not yet identify or deliver all required savings and efficiencies to close the forecast budget gap. The council explicitly states there are 'material risks associated with the delivery of savings, with some schemes already identified as not achieveable.' Interim reliance on one-off reserve use creates short-term flexibility but reinforces the need for sustainable recurring savings.
findings.matters: A lender evaluating medium-term financial resilience needs to see not just a balanced position now, but a credible path to sustainability. Identified savings failures and persistent budget gaps are red flags for future deficit risk.
findings.figures: No specific budget gap figure disclosed in this report; see MTFS for detail
findings.quote: However, the MTFS does not, at this stage, fully identify or deliver all of the savings, efficiencies, income generation opportunities and service transformation measures required to close the forecast budget gap. There are material risks associated with the delivery of savings, with some schemes already identified as not achieveable.

findings.headline: EY must separately assess legality of commercial asset borrowing
findings.detail: Ernst & Young will conduct their own assessment of whether the council's borrowing for purchasing commercial assets was lawful. This review was prompted by concerns previously raised by BDO (the prior auditors).
findings.matters: If the council's borrowing for commercial assets was unlawful, it creates a potential liability and raises questions about governance and financial decision-making.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: EY will need to carry out their own assessment on the legality of borrowing for the purchase of commercial assets as set out by BDO in their reports

findings.headline: Poor quality of the council's working papers is delaying audit completion
findings.detail: EY have identified issues with the quality of working papers the council has provided. The council and auditors are now in discussion to improve the information and evidence standards going forward.
findings.matters: Poor documentation quality suggests weak internal controls and financial record-keeping. This raises concerns about the reliability of the council's financial management.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: The update report also includes some issues around the quality of some of the working papers provided. Discussions have already begun and will continue between the Council and the EY audit team, so that appropriate improvements can be made

findings.headline: Significant audit gaps: entire areas of the accounts cannot be completed
findings.detail: EY have only managed to gain full assurance over some areas and partial assurance in others. Multiple areas will have no audit work completed and will be carried forward to future audits. The last substantial audit work was in 2020/21, which also received a disclaimer opinion.
findings.matters: Unaudited sections of the accounts create financial uncertainty and prevent lenders from assessing the council's true position.
findings.figures: Last substantial external audit work: 2020/21 (received disclaimer opinion). Current audit: partial assurance only on some areas.
findings.quote: there will be a number of areas where work cannot be completed and these will need to be reassessed for the audits in subsequent years

findings.headline: Auditors will not meet statutory deadline and cannot issue normal audit opinion
findings.detail: The 27 February 2026 statutory deadline for publishing audited accounts will be missed. Due to the multi-year audit backlog, EY can only issue a disclaimer opinion, not the normal unmodified opinion. Even then, work will not be completed by April 2026.
findings.matters: A disclaimer opinion means auditors cannot certify the financial statements are accurate. For a lender, this makes it impossible to rely on the council's published accounts.
findings.figures: Statutory deadline: 27 February 2026. Earliest year for unmodified opinion: 2026/27.
findings.quote: it is understood that EY will not meet the current deadline of 27 February for the issuing of their opinion and the accounts will therefore not be able to be finalised. It is hoped that this work will be concluded for the Committee meeting in April

findings.paper_title: Full General Fund Budget and Council Tax setting 2026/27; Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Budget 2026/27
findings.headline: Council will be abolished 1 April 2028 due to Local Government Reorganisation with complete budget reset required and outcome still unknown
findings.detail: Basildon is undergoing LGR with abolition scheduled for 1 April 2028. The council explicitly states that 'Until a formal decision is reached by the Government, the outcome for the Council is unknown. Therefore, the budget has been prepared on the basis that the Council will continue to operate within its current structure for the foreseeable future. It is recognised that the financial position will need to be revised once a clear direction is confirmed.' A £1m reserve has been established for preparatory work, with small spend expected in 2025/26 and bulk utilisation in 2026/27.
findings.matters: LGR creates fundamental uncertainty over Basildon's post-2028 financial position. Lenders need clarity on how existing council debt and liabilities will be handled in the new authority structure.
findings.figures: Abolition date 1 April 2028; £1m LGR reserve established; government decision expected March 2026; preparatory costs anticipated in 2025/26 and 2026/27
findings.quote: The Council is also undergoing a sizeable transformation with Local Government Reorganisation which will result in the abolition of the Council on 1 April 2028.

findings.paper_title: Full General Fund Budget and Council Tax setting 2026/27; Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Budget 2026/27
findings.headline: HRA overspend of £3.2m driven by disrepair case legal costs and compensation payments significantly exceeding approved budget
findings.detail: The HRA is forecast to overspend by £3.2m before application of contingency funding. The council explicitly reports that 'In the current year, the HRA is experiencing financial pressure arising from an increase in disrepair cases. Associated legal costs and compensation payments are significantly exceeding the approved budget.' While some cost overruns in repairs are offset by management underspends, the disrepair liability escalation is uncontrolled within existing budgets.
findings.matters: Unexpected liability exposure in the HRA from disrepair claims indicates either operational quality issues or claims volume shifts. Lenders assess HRA as separate revenue stream; uncontrolled legal and compensation costs threaten HRA sustainability.
findings.figures: £3.2m HRA overspend forecast before contingency; disrepair cases driving cost escalation; legal costs and compensation significantly exceeding approved budget
findings.quote: In the current year, the HRA is experiencing financial pressure arising from an increase in disrepair cases. Associated legal costs and compensation payments are significantly exceeding the approved budget.

findings.paper_title: Full General Fund Budget and Council Tax setting 2026/27; Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Budget 2026/27
findings.headline: Medium-term structural budget gap of £5.6m in 2027/28 growing to £13.2m in 2029/30 with no detailed solutions identified
findings.detail: The council forecasts a £5.6m budget gap in 2027/28 rising to £13.2m by 2029/30. While the council states 'significant work is underway' through transformation programmes and external consultant engagement to identify savings, no specific proposals are detailed for the outer years. The paper explicitly identifies TA demand as the largest contributor to this medium-term deficit.
findings.matters: A structural deficit of this magnitude and trajectory signals the council cannot sustain services at current levels. Multi-year gaps this large indicate the council will exhaust reserves or require major reductions in scope or scope transfers.
findings.figures: £5.6m budget gap 2027/28; £13.2m gap 2029/30; £1m new savings identified for 2026/27; TA identified as largest contributor to deficit
findings.quote: The MTFS position shows a balanced position for 2026/27. However, there remains forecast budget gap of £5.6m in 2027/28, rising to £13.2m in 2029/30.

findings.paper_title: Full General Fund Budget and Council Tax setting 2026/27; Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Budget 2026/27
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation overspend of £5.7m in 2025/26 with 30% annual growth forecast and reserves being depleted to cover it
findings.detail: The General Fund faces a £5.7m overspend in 2025/26, of which £5.5m is driven by temporary accommodation pressure. Nightly paid TA placements have risen by more than a third since April. The council forecasts average annual increases of approximately 30% in TA demand going forward. To cover this year's overspend, the council is using £5m of reserves. While opening 150+ new units in Dartford and exploring other site acquisitions, the council continues to identify expensive nightly lets as a key ongoing financial challenge.
findings.matters: A rapidly growing cost driver that is consuming reserves and will dominate medium-term deficits. Lenders assess whether the council can stabilise this trajectory as reserves deplete and TA costs compound.
findings.figures: £5.7m General Fund overspend 2025/26; £5.5m from TA; nightly paid arrangements risen by more than a third; forecast average annual increase approximately 30%; £5m of reserves drawn down; 150+ units opening in Dartford
findings.quote: General Fund outturn for 2025/26 is forecast to be £5.7m overspent, driven predominantly by pressures in TA, which accounts for £5.5m of the variance.

findings.headline: Council explicitly acknowledges that operating without a permanent Section 151 Officer poses material governance and financial risk.
findings.detail: The Risk Management section states that the absence of a designated Section 151 Officer creates material governance and financial risk, specifically: weakened financial oversight, reduced assurance on budget management, increased risk of non-compliance with legal and regulatory requirements, potential undermining of financial reporting accuracy, and heightened risk of financial mismanagement. The paper also warns that failure to fill the post could lead to external intervention and reputational harm.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether these risks materialised during the 11-month vacancy and what remedial measures are being taken to restore robust financial controls.
findings.figures: None stated
findings.quote: The lack of a designated Section 151 Officer poses a material governance and financial risk to the authority. Without a statutory Chief Finance Officer, the Council is exposed to weakened financial oversight, reduced assurance on budget management, and an increased risk of non‑compliance with legal and regulatory requirements.

findings.headline: Section 151 Officer role was vacant for 11 months, from March 2025 until February 2026, with only interim coverage.
findings.detail: The previous Executive Director of Resources and Governance and Section 151 Officer resigned in March 2025. The statutory finance role was held on an interim basis by the Assistant Director of Finance and Governance until Tim Sams's appointment takes effect on 24 February 2026. An 11-month gap in the permanent chief finance leadership during a period of sustained budget pressure across English councils merits scrutiny into whether governance or financial control issues emerged.
findings.matters: A lender would want to know whether any governance failures, audit findings, or control weaknesses surfaced during an extended vacancy in the top finance post, and what evidence exists that financial oversight remained adequate.
findings.figures: 11 months (March 2025 to February 2026)
findings.quote: Since the resignation of the previous Executive Director of Resources and Governance and Section 151 (Chief Financial) Officer in March 2025, the statutory role of Section 151 Officer has been filled on an interim basis by the Assistant Director of Finance and Governance.

findings.headline: The government's phased approach means Basildon will not receive an unmodified audit opinion before the 2026/27 accounts at the earliest, with reduced-scope audits and modified opinions in the interim.
findings.detail: Due to pandemic-related audit backlogs, the government introduced a phased approach allowing external auditors to issue disclaimer and modified opinions until 2026/27. Audits of financial statements will have reduced scope during this period to reflect system-wide backlog rather than management failings. This means Basildon faces another 18 months minimum of governance assurance gaps.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand that the council's audit assurance will remain incomplete for at least another 18 months, and the commercial property borrowing dispute remains unresolved during this extended gap.
findings.figures: Unmodified audit opinions not expected before 2026/27 accounts.
findings.quote: under this approach, external auditors aim to provide an unmodified audit opinion no earlier than the 2026/27 accounts

findings.headline: Basildon has not received a clean audit opinion since November 2020 and has disclaimer opinions for three consecutive years (2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23).
findings.detail: The council's 2020/21 audit received a disclaimer opinion because BDO had insufficient time to complete matters outstanding, mainly post balance sheet events. Work on 2021/22 and 2022/23 was not undertaken by the external auditor following the legal issue raised in 2020/21, so disclaimer opinions were issued for those years too. A disclaimer opinion means the auditor could not obtain sufficient audit evidence to conclude that accounts are free from material and pervasive misstatements.
findings.matters: Three years without clean audit assurance creates a significant governance gap that affects stakeholder confidence, lender assessment of financial controls, and the reliability of financial reporting.
findings.figures: Last clean audit opinion: November 2020 for 2019/20. Disclaimer opinions for 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23 (three consecutive years).
findings.quote: Basildon Borough Council has not received an audit opinion on any annual statement of accounts since November 2020, which related to the 2019/20 financial year

findings.headline: Auditors concluded that borrowing to finance commercial property purchases in 2020/21 was unlawful; the council disputes this and says it has legal authority for the investment.
findings.detail: BDO's audit identified that borrowing undertaken to finance two investment properties purchased in November 2020 was unlawful. The council contests this, arguing that four properties purchased in 2018/19 were audited without similar challenge, that it obtained external legal counsel in February 2018 concluding the activity was permitted, and that it disclosed the departure from the Prudential Code in its approved Capital & Investment Strategy. The council has disposed of one asset (Solihull) and holds an earmarked reserve to cover rental shortages, but an agreed resolution cannot be found and the matter will be reported to Full Council.
findings.matters: A fundamental disagreement with auditors about the lawfulness of major borrowing raises credit risk, can affect borrowing costs and credit ratings, undermines governance assurance, and creates reputational risk with lenders.
findings.figures: Six commercial properties purchased: one May 2018, three in 2018/19, two in November 2020. One property (Solihull) disposed of.
findings.quote: both the audit report for 2020/21 and the AAR report contain a recommendation regarding the funding of the commercial properties purchased during 2020/21. The external auditor's view is that borrowing undertaken to finance investment properties was unlawful. The Council does not agree with this assessment

news_drafts.headline: All new borrowing is short-term from other local authorities; no long-term PWLB funding accessed
news_drafts.lead: Reliance on short-term inter-authority borrowing exposes the council to rollover risk and interest rate exposure; prevents locking in long-term fixed rates.

news_drafts.headline: Housing Revenue Account capital works delayed following Morgan Sindall contract extension
news_drafts.lead: Capital delivery delays indicate execution risk and could signal further slippage; affects council's ability to meet tenant needs and asset management targets.

news_drafts.headline: Housing Disrepair audit identified major control gaps on Pre-Action Protocol and Awaab's Law compliance, due September 2026
news_drafts.lead: Awaab's Law compliance is a statutory duty for housing maintenance; gaps here expose the council to regulatory enforcement, tenant litigation, and liability. Poor resource allocation to disrepair cases signals inability to manage a core housing function.
